name: Caddy
summary: A self-contained Go web server whose core loads and swaps JSON configurations, composes registered modules through lifecycle contexts, and provides automatic HTTPS as a standard application capability.

features.name: Module-registered extensible core
features.description: Caddy's core manages configuration while modules provide applications, handlers, commands, storage, and other capabilities. A module registers a namespaced ID and constructor; importing a package registers the module in the static binary without dynamic linking.
benefits: Keeps deployment to one self-contained binary
Allows independently developed modules to extend configuration and behavior
Provides a stable namespace and constructor boundary for extension discovery
costs: Extensions must be compiled into the binary and versioned together
Module IDs and interface contracts become compatibility boundaries
Static composition moves plugin selection into the build process

features.name: Provision, validate, use, and cleanup lifecycle
features.description: When Caddy loads a module, it constructs and decodes the module, provisions it, validates it, uses it through the host interface, and invokes cleanup when the containing context is canceled. Failed provisioning or validation also triggers cleanup for resources already acquired.
benefits: Makes initialization and resource release phases explicit
Lets modules reject invalid configuration before serving traffic
Provides cleanup on partial setup failures
costs: Module authors must make provisioning and cleanup safe across failure paths
Nested host and guest modules expand lifecycle ordering concerns
Configuration validity can depend on interactions among modules

features.name: Atomic configuration replacement
features.description: Caddy provisions a new configuration before replacing the current one. Once the new configuration starts successfully, the active context is swapped and the old applications are stopped and cleaned up; configuration is treated as an immutable unit for reload rather than being mutated in place on the hot path.
benefits: Allows granular API edits to produce a whole validated configuration
Avoids interruption when the new configuration can be provisioned and started
costs: For a brief interval old and new configurations may both be operational
Reload success depends on complete provisioning and startup of the new graph
State that must survive reload needs explicit global or usage-pool ownership

features.name: Automatic HTTPS as application behavior
features.description: Caddy's HTTP application integrates automatic HTTPS behavior, including certificate acquisition and renewal workflows, as part of the server's standard application configuration rather than as a separate daemon.
benefits: Makes certificate lifecycle part of the server configuration model
Reduces manual setup for common HTTPS deployments
Allows TLS automation to participate in the same module and storage boundaries
costs: Certificate issuance and renewal introduce external availability dependencies
TLS defaults and automation must be understood when deploying a server
Certificate state requires durable storage and careful reload behavior

mathematical_views.question: How do JSON module IDs, host-child relationships, constructors, and interface assertions form a runnable Caddy application graph?
assumptions: Registered module IDs identify vertices in namespaces
Host modules create and use guest modules through interface boundaries
The graph abstracts Go type details while retaining registration and lifecycle edges

mathematical_views.question: When does a candidate configuration become active, and how are the old applications retired?
assumptions: A candidate passes decode, provision, validation, and startup transitions
The active pointer changes only after the candidate starts successfully
The model does not infer durability or zero-downtime behavior for failed external dependencies

mathematical_views.question: Which state is owned by a configuration context, and which state must be shared or retained across reloads?
assumptions: Most module state is associated with the configuration context that provisions it
Explicit global facilities such as usage pools represent state intended to survive local changes
The view distinguishes ownership structure from a proof of leak freedom

benefits: Self-contained deployment with broad compile-time extension points
costs: Plugin selection and compatibility are coupled to the built binary

benefits: Explicit validation and cleanup boundaries for nested modules
costs: Every extension must implement failure-safe lifecycle behavior

benefits: Consistent whole-configuration reloads with a small synchronization boundary
costs: Concurrent old/new lifetimes and cross-reload state require resource discipline

benefits: Integrated certificate automation for common HTTPS deployments
costs: External issuance, renewal, and durable certificate state affect availability
